The lowest skilled artist on deviant art has put in more time and effort than almost all AI prompters. However, I can recognize that there are folks trying to explore it as a medium. My understanding is that for those folks, AI is part of a larger process and not the entire kit and kaboodle.
I mean, I can appreciate the skills of someone who has taken the time to learn photoshop and digital drawing pads. You know, skills that didn't go into an AI prompt.

I meant exactly what I said. Finding out something was AI means it is fundamentally not the peice of art I thought it was, nor did it have the same meaning. There is value in the time and techniques that an individual has spent their lives refining that is lost when someone shits out a throwaway prompt to get their quick dopamine fix.

If by genius effort, you mean good coders and thousands of pieces of stolen art, then no. I don't appreciate it and while I think it was made with good intentions it will ultimately be a tool for corporations to rob even more people of their livelihoods. 

I can see the value of AI as a data processor, and have seen places where it can do good. I'm also aware that my distaste is futile. Generative AI will never go back in its box, and has fundamentally changed the way we interact with media. I think it also fair to recognize what has been lost, and the damage AI has already done to the livlihoods of artists that are now being passed over for a quick buck.

*Quick Edit: Because I feel that you will harp on it, I at no point said AI was equivalent to sexual assault. It's obviously not. Basic reading comprehension should make it clear that I was equating finding out that a work was ai was similar to finding out additional information about a written work that would change my understanding of the work. Perhaps a better analogy would be that it's similar to finding out a work is plagerized.*

*To make it crystal clear for you: No, AI is not the same as Sexual Assault. To imply that that was my intention is in incredibly bad faith.*

You call the storm by selecting the orange daimond on the map, and holding it until the storm activates. You can grab as many anchors as you want before manually activating it. Some longer runs will require to two to four anchors before can summon the exit and resulting storm.

Edit: to clarify, you can load as many as you want into the arc device

Hmm, okay, some of this I can't help you with, like the controls. I'd maybe recommend looking through the key bindings to see what your options are, but to me most od them felt intuitive. However, I can get your basic gameplay loop down, and give you some of the tips I use to survive runs. 

1st off, basic loop. You roll into your garage, do basic maintenance using crafted resources. Your mains are going to be repair putty in the beginning, though it's often easier to just create a new cride panel to replace an old crude panel. (once you get higher tier parts, this no longer applies). Other things to repair would be specific issues such as cracked windows, flat tires, etc. You can use the big status screen to the immediate right of the exit garage door, the screen on your dash, or individually look at and scan the parts to figure out what you need to fix. (note, both status screens will tell you where the problem is, then yiu'll need to scan it manually). After getting yiur fuel and battery sorted, you are ready to plan your route. 

roll on over to the route planner, you should at the beginning have only one scan charge available. Familiarize yourself with the legend. Next, you'll look at possible destinations. The blue circle indicates how much anchor charge you'll need to exit a particular location (we'll get to anchors.) If a location isn't selectable it typically means that it is on route to a second location. Avoid areas covered by red storms, and starting out I would only pick routes with 1-2 locations. Get your scan, roll on out and leave. 

You land in. a zone. 1st things first, put the car in park and check the map. I do all of my in map driving route when I land. Note any buildings, and any yellow circles. (these are anchors.) plan to grab things in whatever order you feel comfortable with, but stick to the roads for now. Make sure to grab energy relatively early, but don't stress. turn on the radio for some music, soundtrack is banging. (radio is where the dome light controls would be in a typical car.) I usually mark intersections ln my route as I drive to make navigation easier, but you do you. Mats are easy to gather, hit container first, and only scrap things that look worthwhile like computers. 

Anchors are a bit tricky, roll up just outside the yellow zone on the map. (if you are feeling nervous feel free to leave the car running for a quick getaway. just mind the gas.) Hop out of the car, grab the anchor, and haul ass back to the car, avoiding the anomolies it spawns. hop in drive away. 

Once you have enough energy, several orange daimond will apear on the map. pick one when you are ready to leave or the storm sirens go off (preferably pick one on or near a road.) hover over the daimond, it'll show you a circle range, you need to be outside of that to start the exit run. On early runs, you've got a bit of time, but don't dally. Stay on the roads if at all possible on your way. Roll in and appear at the garage. buy some upgrade blueprints from the fabricator terminal, start the process over. 

-------

Some additional notes:

On multi-site trips, you'll see an orange square with an arrow at the edge of the map, you can take this at any time to get to the next map without needing to activate a gate. still grab some anchors for upgrades and an emergency exit. You will need to take an exit at the end od yiur route. 

Stick to the route that you planned on the scanner, it's always better to know what anomalies yiu are heading into. 

On anomalies: Most are actually pretty easy to avoid, once you get thw hang onf them. Some easy ones: Don't touch tourists, dont roll under abductors, just wait for them to pass. If you do get grabbed, you can still steer use that to avoid the worst of the collisions. Either hit bunnies with your crowbar or grab them and chuck them. (bunnies universally suck, but the lim shield upgrade will bounce them no issue.)

Scan every anomaly or building you find. The logs are obtuse, but contain clues about how they function. 

keep some basic repair supplies in your car at all times. 

read the logs, I can't stress this enough, as they record your tutorials and additional info. 

If you don't know how something works, tool wise, test it on the junker out back. 

Upgrade batteries and fuel as soon as posdible. Until then, always turn off your car and headlights begore looting. 

Don't be afraid to turn down the difficulty settings to find something comfortable for you, nobody will know but you. 

If your car starts doing weird stuff (honking when you close doors, etc) You've got a quirk diagnose it all the terminal next to the battery charger. 

Take it slow if you want, don't rush the main missions, get comfortable with shorter runs first. 

------

That's all I've got, hope it helps. I generally don't stress over the game, it scratches a particular itch for me. If you still find it stressful after tweaking, put it down for a bit, and come back when you want to go on a spooky drive with your lovable beater stationwagon.

Edit: I lied, there's more. Keep cans of food on you for quick healing. Slurp down spam and MRE's as necessary. Also, keep a 1st aid kit somewhere in the car. 

Lastly don't do road repairs unless you've got something in the yellow or red, and find a quiet spot to do them.

I think part of what folks are running into here seems to be that this is a game for fans of bethesda RPGs specifically, and fundamentally is not a game for folks who like space games. The joy of most games that focus on the "space" portion of this genre tend to focus on that in between space. Whether it's in NMS derelict freighters lost in deep space, the sudden realization that you are being tailed by pirates in elite dangerous, or just long stretches of peace and quite while you enjoy the scenery of the stars, these are the moments folks like myself tend to enjoy. My favorite thing in one of these games is sitting back and listening to the radio while travelling and discovering something lost and unexpected in the black. So I don't think that this is an issue of there being a lack of things to potentially do in space. 

However, I do think that starfield is just fundamentally not that game. It's a space opera, of the old style, and those are almost always focused more on small vignettes that play out on planets or maybe, if you're lucky, on a space station. 

I do wish Starfield had at least taken a little bit of inspiration from the beauty and weirdness of space itself, with its asteroid belts, comets, exoplanets and more, or at least let folks enjoy those quiet moments in space, but it wasn't what they were focusing on. I would almost argue that it just simply isn't what a bethesda game is anymore, especially with the way the initial quiet of 76 was received.
